entries.name: Potato
entries.wild_ancestor: Solanum brevicaule complex (S. bukasovii and relatives)

domesticated.where: Andes of southern Peru / NW Bolivia

entries.spread: Europe in the 1530s; worldwide by 1800
entries.notes: Third most-consumed food after rice and wheat. Domesticated once, ~6000-10000 years ago, from bitter wild tubers.

entries.name: Cassava (manioc, yuca)
entries.spread: Portuguese to Africa and Asia in the 1500s
entries.notes: Staple of the tropics; bitter varieties carry cyanogenic glucosides and must be peeled, grated, soaked or cooked.

entries.name: Sweet potato

domesticated.where: tropical America (Central vs South America debated)

entries.spread: Polynesia before 1200 CE; to Europe/Asia via Columbus, 1500s
entries.notes: Carried by Polynesian voyagers across the Pacific long before Columbus; a different family and crop to the potato.

entries.name: Taro (cocoyam)
entries.spread: Pacific with the Lapita expansion; Africa about 2000 years ago
entries.notes: Among the oldest cultigens; mother corm, side corms and leaves are all eaten, cooked. Acrid raw.

entries.name: White yam (guinea yam)
entries.spread: to the Caribbean and Americas by the 1500s; world yam staple
entries.notes: The yam of West African festivals and of ifu/fufu; stakes and mounds shape its fields. Tubers reach several kg.

entries.name: Greater yam (ube, water yam)
entries.spread: Austronesian/Lapita into the Pacific; Africa and Caribbean 1500s on
entries.notes: A sterile clonal cultigen of Kuk Swamp antiquity; purple 'ube' is the Filipino dessert yam. Tuber dating uncertain.

entries.name: Chinese yam (shan yao)
entries.spread: East and Southeast Asia; medicines and cuisine
entries.notes: Long, straight, slimy-when-cut root used in TCM ('shan yao') and in mountain yam soups and desserts.

entries.name: Carrot
entries.wild_ancestor: Daucus carota (wild carrot, Queen Anne's lace)
entries.spread: Arab trade to Europe by the 12th century; orange selected in the Netherlands, 17th century
entries.notes: First carrots were purple and yellow; orange arrived late in Dutch breeding. A cool-climate biennial grown as an annual.

entries.name: Beetroot (garden beet)
entries.spread: Europe in the Middle Ages; sugar beet bred 1747-1784
entries.notes: One species, three crops: chard (leaf), beetroot (root), sugar beet (industry). Swollen roots documented by 500 BCE.

entries.name: Turnip
entries.spread: Roman and Byzantine world; staple of medieval Europe
needs: quick steady growth to avoid woody roots
entries.notes: The fodder and table root of antiquity; oil also pressed from its seed. Domesticated location and date are genuinely uncertain.

entries.name: Radish (daikon)
entries.spread: Mediterranean antiquity; Japan developed the giant daikon
entries.notes: Days-from-seed-to-plate in 3-4 weeks for smalls; the Japanese daikon routinely tops 30 cm. Cultivated since Egyptian antiquity.

entries.name: Rutabaga (swede, neep)
entries.wild_ancestor: natural hybrid of kale (Brassica oleracea) and turnip (B. rapa)
entries.spread: Scotland and northern England 18th century; Canada and US
entries.notes: First described in 1620; 'neeps and tatties' with haggis. A kale-turnip hybrid with yellower flesh than turnip.

entries.name: Parsnip
entries.spread: Roman world onward; northern Europe staple before the potato
entries.notes: Sweeter after frost; Roman 'pastinaca' may have meant parsnip or carrot. A Roman-legion winter ration.

entries.name: Celeriac (root celery)
entries.spread: northern European cuisine from the 17th century
entries.notes: The 'knob' is a swollen hypocotyl, not a tuber. Celery's slow, dense cousin; needs ~5 months.

entries.name: Jerusalem artichoke (sunchoke)
entries.spread: France 1605; Europe before the potato; renewed interest for inulin
entries.notes: Sunflower's cousin; tubers are ~16% inulin, not starch — hence the wind it is notorious for. Not from Jerusalem.

entries.name: Ginger
entries.spread: India and China in antiquity; Rome; spice-road staple
needs: warm humid shade or dappled light
entries.notes: A sterile triploid cultigen with no known wild provenance; among the oldest traded spices. Flowers are rare.

entries.name: Turmeric
entries.spread: South and Southeast Asia in antiquity; worldwide via trade
entries.notes: Curcumin: dye, medicine and sacred powder ('haldi'). Like ginger, mostly propagated by rhizome division.

entries.name: Lotus root (renkon)
entries.spread: Asia wherever ponds were farmed; Buddhist monasteries spread it
needs: shallow warm pond or flooded field
entries.notes: Every part is edible; the rhizome cross-sections are crisp with lace holes. Sacred in Buddhism and Hinduism; cultivation dating uncertain.

entries.name: Chinese water chestnut (ma-tai)
entries.spread: China and tropical Asia; canned worldwide for stir-fries
entries.notes: Not a chestnut but a sedge; the 'corm' stays crisp after cooking. Peeling reveals the ivory coin slices of stir-fries.

entries.name: Konjac (elephant yam)

domesticated.where: Yunnan / NE India region, then China

entries.spread: China to Japan ('konnyaku'); health-food noodles worldwide
entries.notes: Glucomannan 'shirataki' noodles; corms are toxic raw (calcium oxalate) and must be processed into jelly. Crop cycle, not season days.

entries.name: Elephant foot yam
entries.spread: India, Bangladesh, SE Asia; feast-day yam curries
entries.notes: Accumulates acrid calcium oxalate — must be boiled long. A prestige festive vegetable in Kerala and Tamil Nadu.

entries.name: Maca (Peruvian ginseng)
entries.spread: local to a few Peruvian high plateaus; exported as powder since the 1990s
entries.notes: Grows where almost nothing else does. Famed as an adaptogen and stamina food; clinical evidence is modest.

entries.name: Oca
entries.spread: Andes for millennia; New Zealand and Europe from the 19th century
entries.notes: Sour from oxalic acid; sun-drying sweetens it. Tastes somewhere between sorrel and a lemon potato; colors from yellow to purple.

entries.name: Ulluco
entries.spread: Andes for millennia; minor crop elsewhere
entries.notes: Waxy, jewel-toned tubers in stripes of red, orange and yellow; chewy when boiled. Pre-Spanish staple of the high valleys.

entries.name: Mashua (añu)
entries.spread: Andes; revival as a 'superfood'
entries.notes: Nasturtium's tuber-bearing cousin, with a peppery bite. Traditional Andean medicine claims it suppresses male libido; evidence thin.

entries.name: Yacón
entries.spread: Andes for centuries; health-food syrup market since the 1990s
entries.notes: Sweet, crisp, mostly fructooligosaccharide (inulin-like) — not starch. Eaten raw; pressed for 'diet' syrup. Pre-Columbian origin, poor records.

entries.name: Yam bean (jicama)
entries.spread: to China and SE Asia by the 1600s; 'lo bak' of Chinese cuisine
entries.notes: Crisp ivory root, eaten raw with chilli and lime. Seeds contain rotenone and are insecticidal — the root is safe.

entries.name: Arrowroot
entries.spread: Caribbean to England for starch; lost ground to cassava and potato starch
entries.notes: Pure, easily digested starch for babies and invalids. Name from Arawak use of the root against arrow poison; now mainly starch powder.

entries.name: Tannia (malanga, yautia)
entries.spread: tropical America; West Africa and Asia since the 1600s; 'cocoyam'
entries.notes: Both corm and leaves are cooked as 'cocoyam'. Big, starchy, filling; blander than taro and more forgiving in wet ground.

entries.name: Tiger nut (chufa)
entries.spread: Mediterranean; Valencian 'horchata de chufa'; Nigerian snack 'aya'
needs: weed control — it is a sedge
entries.notes: Found in pharaonic tombs; a sweet, nutty sedge tuber. Not a nut; the milk gives horchata its name in Spain.

entries.name: Burdock (gobo)
entries.spread: China and Japan; Japan is the only country to eat the root widely
needs: deep fertile soil for the long taproot
entries.notes: Japan's 'gobo': a long crisp taproot for burdock kinpira. Its clinging burrs inspired Velcro. Mild, earthy; a prebiotic fiber bomb.

entries.name: Skirret
entries.spread: Roman and medieval gardens; all but vanished by 1900
entries.notes: Sweet clustered knobby roots, once called 'mountaineer's sugar'. A Roman-medieval favorite eclipsed by the potato and carrot.

entries.name: Salsify (oyster plant)
entries.spread: Mediterranean to northern Europe by the 16th century
entries.notes: Said to taste of oysters; porcini-purple shaving-brush flowers open mornings only. Cultivated since antiquity per botanical tradition.

entries.name: Scorzonera (black salsify)
entries.spread: southern Europe from the 16th century; Germany and Belgium favor it
entries.notes: Black skin, white flesh, milder than salsify and far more cold-hardy. Named for a supposed cure for viper bites; introduced from Spain ~1600.

entries.name: Arrowhead (kuwai, ci gu)
entries.spread: China to Japan ('kuwai'); aquatic 'lotus root' of New Year dishes
entries.notes: Aquatic 'arrowhead'; the curved corms with purple bud tips are auspicious in Japanese New Year cooking. Crisp like water chestnut.

entries.name: Crosnes (Chinese artichoke)
entries.spread: China; an edible curiosity in France since 1882
needs: harvest when frost kills the tops
entries.notes: Pearly, ringed, crunchy little tubers — 'Japanese artichoke' of high-end French cooking. Bland if undercooked; sadly invasive-prone.

entries.name: Camas
entries.spread: never widely farmed; foraged and managed in the Northwest
needs: slow cooking in earth ovens (24-48 h)
entries.notes: The staple 'kamas' of Plateau peoples, cooked for a day or two in earth ovens to caramelize the inulin. Bulb, not tuber, but a classic 'root food'.

entries.name: Groundnut (Indian potato)
entries.spread: never scaled; rediscovered by permaculture and survival gardening
entries.notes: A nitrogen-fixing vine whose underground 'potatoes' grow in strings; up to ~30% protein plus starch. The original American potato.
